708.title: A roll of honor
708.hook: Var 11 lists the Sikhs of the Gurus by name and town, ordinary people remembered (Bhai Gurdas, Var 11)
708.howItsDone: Sikhs read Bhai Gurdas's eleventh var as a record of the early sangat, and it's read and sung alongside the Gurus' bani in some gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru bows to the disciple, and your line, the teacher bows. Who did you ask to teach you something? Day seven hundred eight.

On the wall of an old school hallway, or a fire station, or a village hall, there's often a board with names painted on it in gold. Hardly anyone stops to read it. But somebody once decided those names should outlast the people. Bhai Gurdas made a board like that, out of verse. One of his vars stops telling the stories of the Gurus and starts telling the names of the people who sat with them. Today: a roll of honor.
screen: `NAMES PAINTED IN GOLD.` → `HARDLY ANYONE STOPS TO READ THEM.` → `A BOARD MADE OUT OF VERSE.`

segments.voice: It's his eleventh var. Bhai Gurdas begins with the sangat, the gathering of the Guru's Sikhs, and what a Sikh of the Guru is like. Then he does something a reader might not expect. He starts listing names. Sikh after Sikh, Guru by Guru, he names the people who came to Guru Nanak, then to the Gurus after him. Often a name comes with something attached: the town they came from, their family, their trade, a nickname their neighbors would have known. Read it and you meet a crowd of ordinary people. Not kings, not famous holy men. People with work to do and towns to go home to. Why would a poet spend so many stanzas on a list? Here's one way to hear it. A story about a great teacher can make the followers into a blur, a background crowd that nods. Bhai Gurdas refuses the blur. For him, the sangat isn't scenery around the Guru. It's made of particular people, each worth a line, each one named the way their own town would have named them. There's a second thing going on. A list like this is a kind of witness. These people were there. They heard the Guru's word, carried it home, and lived it in their own streets. The roll says: the path was walked by people like this, in places like that. And a third thing. In the Guru's house, a name on the roll doesn't depend on rank. In Bhai Gurdas's list, being remembered comes from being a Sikh of the Guru. That's the whole qualification. Your own town's board works the same way: you don't have to know the names to feel the weight of them.
screen: `THE ELEVENTH VAR: A LIST OF NAMES.` · `A NAME, A TOWN, A TRADE.` · `THE SANGAT IS NOT A BLUR.` · `A ROLL THAT DOESN'T ASK RANK.` · then, large: `ORDINARY NAMES REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the names of your people. Use the sit to make your own roll. Not famous people. The ones who carried you. A grandmother. A coach. The neighbor who fed you after school. A teacher whose name you nearly forgot. Say each name slowly in your head, and add what Bhai Gurdas would add: where they were from, what they did with their hands. When the bell ends, write the names down somewhere you'll see them. If you pray, you can hold each name for a breath. The bell holds the time.
A roll of honor. Bhai Gurdas's eleventh var, naming the Sikhs of the Gurus one by one, often with their town or trade.
Your line: ordinary names remembered. Today, say one name from your list out loud to someone, and tell them one thing that person did. Day seven hundred eight.

709.title: What a Gursikh does
709.hook: Bhai Gurdas pictures the Sikh who rises early, bathes, remembers, joins the sangat and works honestly
709.howItsDone: Sikh custom keeps the amrit vela, the hours before dawn, for bathing and reciting or listening to the morning banis before the day's work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll of honor, and your line, ordinary names remembered. Whose name did you say out loud? Day seven hundred nine.

What would a stranger learn about you from watching one ordinary day? Not your opinions. Just the day: what time the light went on, what you did first, where you went, how you earned your bread. Yesterday Bhai Gurdas gave us names. Today he gives us the shape of a day, the day of a Sikh who belongs to the Guru. And he doesn't describe it with a list of beliefs. He describes it with a clock. Today's word: Gursikh.
screen: `ONE ORDINARY DAY, WATCHED.` → `NOT OPINIONS, JUST THE DAY.` → `A DAY TOLD BY THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Gursikh puts two words together: Gur, the Guru, and Sikh. A Sikh of the Guru. Bhai Gurdas returns to this person in his vars, and the picture he paints is practical, almost a timetable. The Gursikh rises while the night is still on, in the early hours. Bathes. Then remembers: sits with the Guru's word, with the Name, before the day's noise starts. Then goes to the sangat, the gathering, to sit with others and hear and sing the Guru's hymns. And then goes to work, and earns a living honestly, and shares what comes in. That's it. No mountain top, no cave. A house, a gathering, a workplace. The picture has deep roots in the Guru's own word. In the Guru Granth Sahib, on Ang three hundred five, Guru Ram Das describes the one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru: rising early, bathing, meditating on the Name, and then carrying the Guru's word through the rest of the day. Bhai Gurdas, in his vars, fills in the day around that morning. Turn it over, and three things stand out. First, the order. Remembering comes before the work, so the work happens inside the remembering, not instead of it. Second, the company. The Gursikh's day isn't solitary: the sangat is part of the schedule, not an extra. And third, the money. Honest work is in the picture on purpose. In Bhai Gurdas's picture, holiness doesn't leave the marketplace. It walks into it with clean hands. A Gursikh, in this telling, isn't known by a title. You'd know one by watching the day.
screen: `GUR AND SIKH: A SIKH OF THE GURU.` · `RISE, BATHE, REMEMBER.` · `THE SANGAT, THEN HONEST WORK.` · `KNOWN BY THE SHAPE OF A DAY.` · then, large: `THE GURSIKH'S DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rise a little earlier. Not tonight's resolution, tomorrow's small change. Use the sit to plan it. Pick a time, ten or fifteen minutes before your usual alarm. Picture the house when it's still quiet. Picture what you'll do with those minutes before the phone: wash your face, sit, breathe, read a line that matters to you. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can choose a line of the Guru's word or say Waheguru in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
Gursikh. A Sikh of the Guru. In Bhai Gurdas's vars, someone you'd recognize by the day: rising early, remembering, sitting in the sangat, working honestly.
Your line: the gursikh's day. Tonight, set the alarm a little earlier, and tomorrow, give the first quiet minutes to remembering. Day seven hundred nine.

710.title: One, two, five
710.hook: Bhai Gurdas says one Sikh is a Sikh, two are a sangat, and where five gather the Lord is present (Bhai Gurdas, Var 13)
710.howItsDone: Sikhs gather in sangats of every size, from a family reading together at home to a full gurdwara, and Bhai Gurdas's line is quoted for the worth of even a small gathering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gursikh, and your line, the gursikh's day. Did you find a few quiet minutes before the day began? Day seven hundred ten.

One chair by a window, someone reading alone. A second chair pulled up, and now there's a conversation. Three more, and suddenly it's a gathering, and the room feels different. Nothing about the furniture changed. Bhai Gurdas noticed what changes when people add up, and he put it in a line short enough to say in a single breath, a line that simply counts, the way a child counts on her fingers. Today: one, two, five.
screen: `ONE CHAIR BY A WINDOW.` → `A SECOND CHAIR: A CONVERSATION.` → `FIVE CHAIRS: A GATHERING.`

segments.voice: It's in his thirteenth var. Bhai Gurdas says: one is a Sikh. Two are a sadh sangat, a holy company. And where five are, there is God. Take the steps one at a time. One is a Sikh. Start there, because it's easy to skip. A single person, alone, early in the morning, remembering, is already a Sikh. Nobody needs a crowd to be on the path. Two are a sangat. The moment a second person joins, it's no longer just practice. It's company. Two people reading a line of the Guru's word together, or singing it softly in a kitchen, already make the thing Bhai Gurdas praises in his vars: the sangat. And then, five. Where five gather, he says, God is present. Not that God is absent from the one, or the two. The line climbs, the way a person climbs stairs, and at the top is the plainest promise of the three. Some readers hear in it an old Punjabi way of speaking about a village council of five, where God was said to sit among the five. Some readers also hear it ahead of a moment later in the Sikh story, when five Sikhs stand together at the heart of the Khalsa. Bhai Gurdas doesn't spell out either one. His line simply counts. What's striking is how small his numbers are. He doesn't say a thousand, or a full gurdwara, or a festival crowd. He says five. A gathering that fits around one table. A gathering anyone could make by this weekend. In Bhai Gurdas's arithmetic, the holy company was never about size. It starts with one, becomes real with two, and five is enough.
screen: `ONE IS A SIKH.` · `TWO ARE A SANGAT.` · `WHERE FIVE ARE, THERE IS GOD.` · `SMALL NUMBERS, ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `WHERE FIVE GATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather with two others. Use the sit to pick them. Two people you could sit with this week, at a table, on a call, on a bench. Not for a big event. For something small and shared: a meal, a walk, a song, a reading, a few minutes of quiet together. See their faces. Notice the room change when you picture three chairs instead of one. Then choose the day you'll ask them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for the three of you. The bell holds the time.
One. The first step in Bhai Gurdas's count: one is a Sikh, two are a holy company, and where five are, there is God.
Your line: where five gather. Today, send the message that asks two people to sit with you this week. Day seven hundred ten.

711.title: A hedge round the orchard
711.hook: defending Guru Hargobind's new ways, Bhai Gurdas says an orchard needs a thorny hedge (Bhai Gurdas, Var 26)
711.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind for holding miri and piri together, worldly and spiritual authority, and Bhai Gurdas's twenty-sixth var is read as an early defense of that change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one, two, five, and your line, where five gather. Did you ask two people to sit with you? Day seven hundred eleven.

Nobody plants a hedge of thorns for its own sake. Thorn bushes aren't pretty, and they snag your sleeve. But walk around an old orchard, with fruit hanging low and goats wandering nearby, and the thorns suddenly make sense. They were never there for themselves. They were there for the fruit. Bhai Gurdas reached for exactly that picture when people were troubled by a Guru who didn't look like the Gurus before him. Today: a hedge round the orchard.
screen: `NOBODY PLANTS THORNS FOR FUN.` → `AN ORCHARD, AND GOATS NEARBY.` → `A GURU WHO LOOKED DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: The Guru was Guru Hargobind. Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who took up the sword alongside the Guru's word, and kept horses and armed Sikhs around him. And some people didn't like it. In his twenty-sixth var, Bhai Gurdas sets out what they were saying, and he doesn't soften it. The earlier Gurus sat in the dharamsal, they said, and this one doesn't stay in one place. He keeps dogs. He goes hunting. The Gurus before him gave us hymns; this one doesn't sit and compose them. It's a list of complaints, and Bhai Gurdas lets it stand in full. Then he answers. The truth, he says, can't be hidden, and the Sikhs still gather round the Guru like bees round a lotus. And then the picture that names today. To protect an orchard, you plant a hedge of thorny kikar around it. The hedge isn't the orchard. It isn't the fruit. Nobody walks into an orchard to admire the thorns. But without them, the fruit doesn't survive the season. Hear what Bhai Gurdas is claiming. The swords and horses aren't a change of heart. The orchard is the same one Nanak planted: the Name, the sangat, the Guru's word. The hedge is what keeps it alive in hard times. That's a careful argument, and it holds two things together that people tend to pull apart. Gentleness and protection. A path of humility, and the readiness to defend it. Sikhs speak of this as miri and piri, the worldly and the spiritual held by the same Guru. Bhai Gurdas says it with a gardener's eye.
screen: `A GURU WITH SWORD AND HORSES.` · `THE COMPLAINTS, IN FULL.` · `A HEDGE OF THORNY KIKAR.` · `THE HEDGE IS NOT THE ORCHARD.` · then, large: `A HEDGE FOR THE ORCHARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect one good thing. Use the sit to name it. Something growing in your life that's easy to trample. A morning routine. A friendship that's still new. A child's bedtime story. An hour that's supposed to be yours. Then ask what would keep it safe. Not a wall. A hedge. A small boundary: a phone left in another room, a no said kindly, a time written down. Choose one, and decide where it goes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over the thing you're guarding. The bell holds the time.
A hedge round the orchard. Bhai Gurdas's answer to those troubled by Guru Hargobind's new ways: an orchard needs a thorny hedge to keep the fruit alive.
screen: `A HEDGE ROUND THE ORCHARD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a hedge for the orchard. Today, plant the one small boundary you chose, and notice what grows behind it. Day seven hundred eleven.

712.title: The kabitts
712.hook: Bhai Gurdas also wrote short Braj verses of great beauty
712.howItsDone: Bhai Gurdas's Kabitt Savaiye are studied and recited by Sikhs alongside his vars, and some are sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hedge round the orchard, and your line, a hedge for the orchard. What small boundary did you plant, and what did it protect? Day seven hundred twelve.

Some writers have two voices. The same person who writes a long novel also scribbles tiny poems in the margins, and sometimes it's the tiny ones people carry around. For days now we've been walking through Bhai Gurdas's vars: long ballads, stanza after stanza, telling the story of the Gurus and the sangat. But that wasn't all he wrote. He had a second voice, in a second language, and it was small. Today: the kabitts.
screen: `TWO VOICES, ONE WRITER.` → `THE LONG BALLADS: THE VARS.` → `A SECOND VOICE, SMALL.`

segments.voice: Start with the language. The vars are in Punjabi. The kabitts are in Braj, a language of poetry, written down in the Gurmukhi script Sikhs use for the Guru's word. Bhai Gurdas could move between them. Then the shape. A kabitt is a short, tightly measured stanza. Where a var tells a story across many verses, a kabitt has to say what it says inside one. That changes how it works. A kabitt can't wander. It packs. One way Bhai Gurdas packs is by stacking pictures. As this, so that. As a thing in nature behaves, so a Sikh of the Guru behaves. Comparison after comparison, pressed close together, until the last line lands with all their weight behind it. A kabitt is less like a road and more like a jewel: you turn it over in your hand and the light catches a different face each time. Why does that matter? Because some truths need a story, and some need a stone you can carry. One way to hear it: the vars suit a long evening in the sangat, when there's time for the whole tale. The kabitts suit a pocket. Short enough to learn. Dense enough to keep giving. And there's a quiet lesson in the fact that he wrote both. The same devotion can be told long and told short. A whole life of praise, and a single bright line you can read aloud before the kettle boils.
screen: `PUNJABI VARS, BRAJ KABITTS.` · `ONE TIGHT STANZA.` · `AS THIS, SO THAT.` · `A STORY, OR A STONE TO CARRY.` · then, large: `SMALL AND BRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one of his verses aloud. If you can, find a single kabitt of Bhai Gurdas in a translation you trust, or one stanza of his vars if that's what's at hand. Don't hunt for long. Pick one. Then use the sit to read it slowly, out loud if you can, or under your breath. Read it a second time. Notice one picture in it, and let that picture sit in your mind while the bell runs. If there's no verse nearby, sit with the last line you remember from these lessons. The bell holds the time.
The kabitts. Bhai Gurdas's short verses in Braj, written in Gurmukhi: one tight stanza each, packed with pictures.
Your line: small and bright. Today, carry one short line you love, and read it once more before you sleep. Day seven hundred twelve.

713.title: Bhai Nand Lal
713.hook: a Persian poet and scholar who served at Guru Gobind Singh's court
713.howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Bhai Nand Lal's Persian poems, and Sikh custom allows them, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, in kirtan alongside the Guru's bani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kabitts, and your line, small and bright. Which short line did you carry, and did you read it again before sleep? Day seven hundred thirteen.

Bhai Gurdas has been our guide since this year began, writing in Punjabi and in Braj, close to the Gurus who came before. Now the path hands us to a second teller, from a later court and a different language. He's a learned man who writes in Persian, the language Rumi and Hafiz wrote in, and he spends his gift on Guru Gobind Singh. Sikhs know him by a title of respect, and by a pen name. Today: Bhai Nand Lal.
screen: `A SECOND TELLER.` → `A LATER COURT, A NEW LANGUAGE.` → `PERSIAN, FOR THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Bhai Nand Lal was a poet and a scholar who served at the court of Guru Gobind Singh. Bhai is the same title of respect Bhai Gurdas carries: brother. He wrote under a pen name, Goya, in the Persian manner. And what he wrote, he wrote in Persian. Here's the thing to notice. A court in his world was a place of learning and display, and Persian poetry was a high art, with its own rules, its own pictures, its own long tradition of writing about love for the Divine as a lover writes about the beloved. Nand Lal didn't leave any of that behind when he came to the Guru. He didn't decide that a Sikh had to stop being a poet, or stop writing in the language he'd mastered. He turned the whole art toward the Guru. The lover, the beloved, the beloved's face: in his poems, those old Persian pictures point to the One, and to the Guru who shows the way. That tells you something about the Guru's house. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gathered poets around him, and Nand Lal is one of the names Sikhs remember. His learning wasn't treated as a distraction from devotion. It became a way of devotion. Over the next few days you'll meet some of his writing: a book about life, his love-poems, and writings on conduct that carry his name. Today, just meet the man. A scholar at court, a poet with a pen name, who brought the best thing he had, his Persian, and laid it at the Guru's feet. Sikh custom lets his poems, with Bhai Gurdas's vars, be sung in kirtan.
screen: `A POET AND SCHOLAR AT COURT.` · `PEN NAME: GOYA.` · `PERSIAN PICTURES, TURNED TO THE ONE.` · `LEARNING AS A WAY OF DEVOTION.` · then, large: `THE POET AT COURT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a line of poetry in translation. Find one short line from a poem first written in another language. Persian if you can, or any language not your own. Read it once. Then use the sit to stay with it. Notice what the translator had to choose, and what might have gone missing on the way across. Then think of one gift you have, a skill or a craft or a language, and ask what it would look like turned toward something you love. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Nand Lal. A Persian poet and scholar at Guru Gobind Singh's court, who wrote as Goya and turned his art toward the Guru.
Your line: the poet at court. Today, use one skill you're proud of for something you love, not for show. Day seven hundred thirteen.

714.title: The book of life
714.hook: Nand Lal's Zindagi Nama speaks of the longing to see the Beloved in everything
714.howItsDone: Sikhs read Bhai Nand Lal's Zindagi Nama in Persian and in translation, and its verses are recited and sung as poems of longing for the Divine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Nand Lal, and your line, the poet at court. Which of your gifts did you turn toward something you love? Day seven hundred fourteen.

Someone who's just fallen in love sees the beloved's name on a shop sign. Hears their laugh in a stranger's voice across a train platform. Smells their coat in a crowded elevator. The world hasn't changed. The one looking at it has. Bhai Nand Lal took that ordinary, slightly ridiculous experience and made it into a whole way of seeing, and pointed it at God. He gave the book a plain title. Today: the book of life.

segments.voice: In Persian it's the Zindagi Nama. Zindagi, life. Nama, a book or a letter. The book of life. It's a poem, written in Persian, in the language of love poetry. Here is its center. Nand Lal writes of a longing to see the Beloved, meaning God, and of the strange thing that happens when that longing takes hold: the Beloved begins to show up everywhere, wherever the eye falls. For the one who longs, there's nowhere the Beloved isn't. Turn that over a few ways. First, the longing isn't a problem to be cured. In the Zindagi Nama, wanting to see is itself part of the path. The ache is a kind of attention. Second, the seeing is the reward. Not a vision in a far-off place, not a reward after death. A changed way of looking, here, at ordinary things. Third, it fits the Guru's word Nand Lal knew. Sikhs hear the Guru Granth Sahib speak of the One pervading everything, in every heart, in water and land. Nand Lal says it in the language of a lover who can't stop seeing the beloved's face. And fourth, it's for a life, not a moment. The title says it. This isn't a book about a single experience. It's a book of life, a way to walk through all of it with your eyes open. Nand Lal doesn't promise the longing ever goes quiet. He seems to treat it as a good companion for the whole road.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something with longing. Choose one ordinary thing within reach. A cup. A plant on the sill. The light on a wall. Your own hand. Use the sit to look at it the way a lover looks: slowly, as if it might be about to say something. Don't analyze it. Let it be beautiful if it wants to be. Notice the moment your eyes want to move on, and stay one breath longer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru to what you see. The bell holds the time.
